question: When Church, kings and merchants start to write fats down, what do their rules and ledgers show about oil, butter and the whale?
summary: The Middle Ages divide Europe by fat. For roughly half the year Christians fast, and in the north, where butter and lard are the cooking fats, a Lent without butter is a hardship; in the south oil carries on ([[b1]]). Councils forbid butter in Lent, a duchess lobbies Rome for the right to use it in 1491, and a cathedral tower is said to have been paid for out of butter dispensations ([[o1]], [[o2]], [[b2]]). Butter itself shifts from a sheep's luxury to an everyday cattle fat ([[ec5]]), and oil serves as money in the south ([[ec6]]).

Documents also make other fat economies countable. The Cairo Geniza shows Tunisian oil shipped to Egypt by the skin, Egypt's flax, linseed and sesame oils, and a trade in linseed oil east to Aden ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x2]]); the Song capital counts oil among the seven necessities, with a dozen oils listed, tallow-tree candles, and the first Chinese description of an oil press ([[ec4]], [[th1]], [[te2]], [[te1]]); and the Basques hunt right whales from about AD 1000, selling the blubber as ‘Lenten fat’ until kings begin to tax the whale ([[ec1]], [[o3]]). On the other side of the world, Thule hunters take bowhead whales and burn their oil in lamps across the Arctic ([[ec9]]), and a Fustat shop holds linseed oil and soap among its stock ([[l2]]). Elsewhere a Palermo letter of about 1064 shows a Tunisian merchant trading five thousand dinars of olive oil with Muslim and Jewish partners, a Fustat synagogue accounts for its olive and linseed lamp oil, and a Borneo chronicle lists four Shanghai jars of coconut oil among island trade goods ([[x3]], [[ec11]], [[ec10]]).
Two quieter shifts close the folio: palm oil is on sale on the West African coast by the 1480s ([[ec7]]), and, in China, su drifts from butter toward animal-fat shortening ([[ec8]]).

themes.title: Lent, butter and the oil line
text: The Church's fasting rules, their enforcement and their sale: a geography of fats written into law, built tower by tower.

themes.title: The Mediterranean oil ledgers
text: Geniza documents show the real flows: Tunisian oil to Alexandria, Egyptian linseed to Syria and Aden, sesame in the Delta.

themes.title: Song China's oil economy
text: A dozen oils, the first described press, candles from the tallow tree and a changing meaning for su.

themes.title: The Basque whale and the beginning of whale-oil
text: The first organised whaling, sold for fast-day fat and light and soap, quickly taxed by kings.

themes.title: Beyond Europe, Egypt and China
text: A palm-oil market on the West African coast and the Arctic’s household whale-oil economy, the only entries from outside the folio’s three main worlds.

turning_points.text: The Basques hunt the right whale and sell its fat on fast days.
Five thousand skins of Tunisian oil reach Alexandria in one season.
Wang Zhen describes the Chinese oil press.
The Council of Angers restricts butter in Lent.
The Butter Tower of Rouen is built.
Brittany, then much of northern Europe, wins butter dispensations.

how_to_read: *Order* and *Belief* carry the Lent story; *Economy* and *Exchange* carry the Geniza and the Song. The Nexus ties the fasting rules to the butter dispensations and the whale taxes.
The two halves of the folio (Latin Europe and the Islamic and Chinese worlds) barely touch, and the Overview reads them side by side.
The *picture by region* shows a Europe-and-Egypt-and-China folio; the Americas and Africa have one entry each, and the Thule date is itself contested.

sources.intro: Documents rule this period. The Geniza, the Song miscellany and the Lenten canons are all read through intermediaries — Goitein, Needham and Khosrova — and so inherit their selection.
main: Khosrova, with Flandrin, for Lent and butter ([[b1]], [[o1]], [[o2]], [[b2]]); Mueller for oil as money ([[ec6]]).
Goitein, *A Mediterranean Society* vol. 1, read by OCR, for the Geniza ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x2]], [[l1]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for Song and Yuan China ([[ec4]], [[th1]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[ec8]]).
Ellis for whaling ([[ec1]], [[o3]]); Lynn for palm oil ([[ec7]]).
Goitein again for the shop of 1104 ([[l2]]); museum and encyclopedia pages found by search for the Thule ([[ec9]]).
Goitein vol. II for the Palermo letter and the synagogue accounts ([[x3]], [[ec11]]); Reid for the Borneo chronicle ([[ec10]]); Chang on the Ming reading of su yu ([[ec8]]).
contested: The Rouen tower's financing is tradition without accounts ([[b2]]); the date of the Angers canon is not given ([[o1]]).
Mueller's oil-as-money contracts are unnamed ([[ec6]]); the Butter-to-cattle shift is unsourced ([[ec5]]).
The Muslim scholar's remark on Jewish cake makers is hostile testimony ([[l1]]).
The Thule expansion dates and whaling’s role are argued ([[ec9]]).
gaps: Medieval Italian, Spanish and Provençal oil trade, and soap guilds, have no primary source here.
Vol. 3 of Goitein and Ibn Butlan, Seth and Ibn al-Baytar on fats were not read.

Africa has one entry (West African palm oil in the 1400s); nothing on shea after Kirikongo, Ethiopia, the Swahili coast or Mali. The Americas have the Thule only; Aztec, Maya and Andean fats, India, Central Asia, Southeast Asia and Oceania have no entry.

text: Ten entries on the Church’s fat line and the kings’ whale: Lent, the Council of Angers, Anne of Brittany, the Butter Tower, the Basques and the whale taxes, butter turning into a cattle fat, oil as money, Arab dishes in Latin cookbooks and Spanish oil going north ([[b1]], [[o1]], [[o2]], [[b2]], [[ec1]], [[o3]], [[ec5]], [[ec6]], [[e1]], [[x1]]). Sicily is here too: a Tunisian merchant’s five thousand dinars of oil in Palermo ([[x3]]).

The Geniza: Tunisian oil shipped to Alexandria, Egypt’s flax, linseed and sesame, linseed to Syria and Aden, a Muslim scholar’s remark on Jewish cake makers and a shop’s stock in 1104 ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x2]], [[l1]], [[l2]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy. The synagogue lamp-oil accounts are here too ([[ec11]]).

Song and Yuan China: a dozen oils, the first description of an oil press, Hangzhou’s necessities, tallow-tree candles and su turning into animal-fat shortening ([[th1]], [[te1]], [[ec4]], [[te2]], [[ec8]]). Southeast Asia gets its first entry here: four Shanghai jars of coconut oil in a Banjarmasin chronicle ([[ec10]]).

One entry: palm oil on sale along the West African coast in the 1460s–1480s, as two Portuguese-era writers report it ([[ec7]]). The Tunisian oil in [[ec2]] is filed under the Near East because it is shipped to Egypt. Shea, Ethiopia, the Swahili coast and Mali have no entry; the library holds no source for them.
One entry: Thule whalers and their oil lamps across the Arctic, with the expansion’s date and whaling’s role disputed ([[ec9]]).
